paras: The threatened expulsion of alleged cotton thieves in Oglethorpe County, Georgia, followed the capture in late 1880 of one of two Black men accused of stealing cotton from under George B. Lumpkin's gin house. According to the Oglethorpe Echo, indignant citizens intended to drive the whole alleged band of thieves out of the neighborhood, though no report shows that they did so. The Echo's paragraph circulated through Georgia exchange columns for two weeks in December.
The Echo reported that it had never heard of so much cotton stealing as in recent weeks. Its item placed the alleged band's activity in "that section" during the winter and did not name a town.

In what the Echo called "last week," Lumpkin was said to have found two Black men under his gin house "in the act of stealing cotton." One of them was captured, by whom the item does not say, and he was reported to have exposed "an organized band of cotton thieves." The paper named the band's leader only as an old Black man living on Mid Johnson's Flatwoods place and accused him of having fourteen bales ginned from as many acres of "bumblebee cotton" while selling seed cotton to a neighbor.

"The citizens are indignant," the Echo wrote, "and intend to run the last one of this crowd from their midst." The item does not say what became of the second man, whether the captured man was handed to officers, or whether anyone was driven away.
No report of an expulsion carried out, a magistrate's hearing or a trial connected to Lumpkin's gin house appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News carried the Echo paragraph on December 10, followed by the Columbus Enquirer-Sun on December 14 and The Free Press on December 16. The Athens Banner, the Hartwell Sun and the Home Journal reprinted it between December 21 and 23, each crediting the Echo and adding no comment.

The Echo treated the accusations as established and supported them by pointing to the alleged leader's family, saying he was sending a daughter to boarding school and buying silk dresses for his wife "to wear every day." It reported the citizens' plan to run the group out without criticism, and the papers that reprinted it framed it as ordinary state news alongside fires, deaths and crop reports.

accounts.label: Oglethorpe Echo local item
accounts.gist: Lumpkin caught two Black men stealing cotton under his gin house; one was captured and exposed a band led by an old man on Mid Johnson's place, and indignant citizens intended to drive the whole group out.

framing.detail: The Echo presented the accusations as fact, pointed to the alleged leader's daughter at boarding school and his wife's silk dresses, and reported the citizens' intent to run the group out without criticism.
The Columbus Enquirer-Sun, Athens Banner, Hartwell Sun and Home Journal reprinted the Echo paragraph verbatim in exchange columns.
